identity.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
brand_names: Zuplenz (oral soluble film; discontinued in the United States)

summary: Fast-acting anti-nausea medication that’s commonly used to control nausea from anxiety, panic, or psychiatric medications. Usually works within ~30 minutes. Main watch-outs: constipation, headache, and rare but serious QT prolongation (heart rhythm risk).
description: Ondansetron (Zofran) is a serotonin 5-HT3 blocker that calms nausea and vomiting fast—often within about 30 minutes. In psychiatry, it’s most often used as a “support med” for nausea from SSRIs/SNRIs, stimulants, lithium, opioid withdrawal, or intense anxiety/panic. It’s not sedating for most people, but constipation and headaches are common. It can also prolong the QT interval (a heart rhythm issue), especially with higher IV doses or in people with risk factors—so dosing and interactions matter.
patient_summary: Zofran can shut down nausea fast and help you stay on your psych meds when your stomach is trying to sabotage you. Most people feel relief within about 30 minutes. The tradeoff is usually constipation or headaches. The rare-but-serious risk is QT prolongation (heart rhythm problems), especially with higher IV doses or if you’re on other QT-prolonging meds.

primary.condition_name: Medication-induced nausea (supportive care with psychiatric medications)

secondary.context: Can be used as a symptom-focused option when anxiety shows up in the body as persistent nausea, especially during acute flares.
Helpful for nausea during panic surges (especially when nausea triggers more panic). Not a panic treatment—just stomach support.
Commonly used short-term to get people through SSRI/SNRI start-up nausea so they can actually stay on the medication long enough to benefit.
Sometimes used to reduce nausea during withdrawal (e.g., opioids). This is supportive symptom care, not treatment of the withdrawal syndrome itself.

common_adverse_effects.notes: If you get headaches easily (especially migraine history), you might notice this more. Hydration helps; if headaches are severe or persistent, reassess dosing and alternatives.

Ondansetron can slow gut motility. If you’re already constipation-prone (low fiber, dehydration, opioids, anticholinergics, some psych meds), plan ahead: fluids, fiber, movement, and a clinician-approved bowel regimen if needed.
More likely if you’re dehydrated from nausea, or if you stand up quickly. Hydration and slow position changes help.

serious_risks.risk: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes (rare but serious): higher risk with IV dosing, higher doses, electrolyte abnormalities, underlying heart disease, bradyarrhythmias, or concurrent QT-prolonging meds.
Serotonin syndrome (rare): risk increases when combined with serotonergic agents (e.g., SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs, mirtazapine, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, methylene blue).
Immediate hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis: hives, swelling, wheeze, shortness of breath, hypotension—medical emergency.
Severe constipation/possible bowel obstruction (rare): worsening abdominal pain, no bowel movement, vomiting—seek urgent evaluation.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to ondansetron or any component of the formulation
Concomitant use with apomorphine (risk of profound hypotension and loss of consciousness)

precautions: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes have been reported; risk increases with higher doses and risk factors (electrolyte abnormalities, underlying heart disease, bradyarrhythmias, or other QT-prolonging drugs).
No single IV dose should exceed 16 mg due to QT prolongation risk.
Avoid in congenital long-QT syndrome when possible; treat as a high-risk situation requiring clinician oversight.

Serotonin syndrome has been reported with 5-HT3 antagonists, especially when combined with serotonergic medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, mirtazapine, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, methylene blue). Some reported cases were fatal.
Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, can occur.

interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated: reports of profound hypotension and loss of consciousness.

interactions.interactant: QT-prolonging medications (multiple classes, including some antipsychotics and antidepressants)
interactions.mechanism: Additive QT prolongation risk; higher chance of dangerous arrhythmias in high-risk patients.
interactions.action: Before stacking QT-risk meds, do an interaction check and consider ECG/electrolytes if you have risk factors.

interactions.interactant: Serotonergic medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, mirtazapine, lithium, tramadol, fentanyl, methylene blue)
interactions.mechanism: Serotonin syndrome has been reported with 5-HT3 antagonists, especially with concomitant serotonergic drugs; some cases were fatal.
interactions.action: Monitor for serotonin syndrome symptoms; if symptoms occur, stop and seek urgent care.

interactions.mechanism: Low potassium or magnesium increases QT-related risk.
interactions.action: Correct electrolytes in higher-risk situations, especially if using IV dosing or multiple QT-risk meds.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: ECG when clinically indicated: congenital long-QT, history of arrhythmia, heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, older adults with multiple QT-risk meds, or if giving IV dosing.
Electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) when risk is present: ongoing vomiting/diarrhea, diuretics, malnutrition, or medical illness that increases QT vulnerability.
Serotonin syndrome symptoms when combined with serotonergic meds: agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, diarrhea, fever, hyperreflexia—stop and seek urgent care if suspected.
Hypersensitivity reactions: hives, swelling, wheezing, hypotension—medical emergency.
Bowel function: constipation monitoring, especially if the patient is already prone to constipation or is taking constipating medications (opioids, anticholinergics, some psych meds).
Functional outcome: Are you able to eat, hydrate, and stay on your primary psychiatric treatment plan?

special_populations.pregnancy: Ondansetron may be considered for severe or persistent nausea and vomiting of pregnancy when preferred agents have failed. Safety data are mixed; absolute risk appears low, but some guideline language recommends individualized decision-making—especially before 10 weeks gestation. Dose-dependent QT prolongation is also a consideration, so higher-risk patients may need ECG/electrolyte monitoring.
special_populations.lactation: Ondansetron is present in human milk. Available data suggest infant exposure is low and reported adverse events in studied infants were not observed; breastfeeding is often considered acceptable when the relative infant dose is <10%, but this should be individualized (especially for premature infants or medically fragile infants).
special_populations.geriatric: No routine oral dose adjustment is generally required, but older adults may have higher baseline QT risk (more cardiac disease, more QT-prolonging meds). If QT risk factors exist, consider ECG/electrolyte monitoring.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No dose adjustment is usually necessary because renal clearance accounts for a small fraction of total clearance; dialysis is unlikely to remove significant amounts.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: typically no adjustment; severe hepatic impairment: do not exceed 8 mg/day total.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral absorption with peak around ~2 hours (varies by formulation); oral disintegrating tablets are bioequivalent to tablets and are not absorbed through the oral mucosa
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Oral bioavailability reduced by first-pass metabolism (range varies by patient and setting)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: About 3 to 6 hours in adults; prolonged with hepatic impairment
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily as metabolites in urine and feces
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food may slightly increase absorption; can be taken without regard to meals

dosing.titration: Psychiatry-relevant use is usually PRN nausea control (for medication side effects or anxiety/panic-related nausea). Dosing is individualized—especially if you have QT risk factors or liver disease.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Ondansetron (Zofran) is an anti-nausea medication. In psychiatry, it’s not the main treatment—it’s the sidekick that keeps nausea from derailing your real plan. Think: SSRI start-up nausea, anxiety/panic nausea, or nausea during stressful medication changes.
items: Psych med start-up nausea: Especially with SSRIs/SNRIs, stimulants, or other meds that can upset the stomach early on
Anxiety or panic nausea: When nausea is part of the anxiety loop (and sometimes fuels the loop)
Medication-change nausea: During dose increases, switches, or tapers when your GI system is extra reactive
Supportive care: Keeping hydration and nutrition stable when nausea is threatening your ability to function
off_label: Severe or persistent nausea in pregnancy when preferred first-line options have failed (requires individualized risk/benefit, especially early pregnancy)
Acute severe nausea/vomiting in urgent settings (symptom relief)

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Ondansetron is usually a fast relief medication for nausea.
key_points: About 30 minutes: Many people start feeling nausea relief
Around 2 hours: Oral forms often reach peak levels (varies by formulation)
Every 8 to 12 hours: Common PRN spacing when symptoms persist
3 to 6 hours: Typical adult half-life (can be much longer with liver impairment)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: In psychiatric care, ondansetron is mainly used as a practical tool: reduce nausea enough to keep you hydrated, eating, and able to continue the medication or treatment plan that’s actually targeting anxiety, panic, or mood.
sections.clinical_details: This medication’s strongest evidence base is in prevention and treatment of nausea/vomiting in medical settings (e.g., chemotherapy, postoperative care). Psychiatry-relevant use is typically supportive—managing nausea from anxiety physiology or medication side effects so adherence and functioning improve.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: QT prolongation risk: avoid high IV single doses and be careful if you’re on other QT-risk meds.
other: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes have been reported; risk increases with higher doses and risk factors (electrolyte abnormalities, underlying heart disease, bradyarrhythmias, or other QT-prolonging drugs).
No single IV dose should exceed 16 mg due to QT prolongation risk.
Avoid in congenital long-QT syndrome when possible; treat as a high-risk situation requiring clinician oversight.

Serotonin syndrome has been reported with 5-HT3 antagonists, especially when combined with serotonergic medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, mirtazapine, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, methylene blue). Some reported cases were fatal.
Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, can occur.
patient_counseling: Tell your clinician if you have a history of long QT, fainting spells, heart rhythm issues, heart failure, or low potassium/magnesium.
If you’re on multiple meds that can prolong QT (common in psychiatry), ask for an interaction check before you stack them.
Seek urgent care for: fainting, racing/irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness, or chest symptoms.
Know serotonin syndrome red flags if you’re on serotonergic meds: agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle stiffness, diarrhea, fever—get urgent help.
If you’ve ever had a serious allergic reaction to ondansetron, don’t re-challenge without medical supervision.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: headache and constipation. Less commonly: dizziness or drowsiness (more noticeable with IV use in some settings). Rare but serious: QT prolongation/arrhythmias and hypersensitivity reactions.
plain_language_list: Rare: abnormal heart rhythm (QT prolongation), allergic reactions

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Psychiatry-relevant use is usually PRN nausea control (for medication side effects or anxiety/panic-related nausea). Dosing is individualized—especially if you have QT risk factors or liver disease.

adult.nausea_prn_oral: 4 to 8 mg PO as a single dose; may repeat every 8 to 12 hours as needed (common PRN strategy when nausea is blocking meals, hydration, or medication adherence).
adult.nausea_prn_severe_or_persistent: 4 to 8 mg PO every 8 hours as needed for a short window (e.g., during SSRI/SNRI initiation). Use the lowest effective dose and reassess if you need it continuously.
adult.parenteral_prn: 4 mg IV as a single dose in monitored settings when oral dosing is not possible; repeat dosing should follow institutional protocols and QT-risk assessment.
adult.max_iv_single_dose: No single IV dose should exceed 16 mg due to QT prolongation risk.
adult.hepatic_severe_max_daily: If severe hepatic impairment: maximum total daily dose 8 mg (all routes).

sections.simple_explanation: For most people in psychiatric care, ondansetron is a short-term or as-needed tool: take it when nausea threatens eating, hydration, or staying on your medication plan. The major safety rule is to respect QT risk—especially with IV dosing or when you’re on other QT-risk meds.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Ondansetron crosses the placenta and is present in breast milk. In psychiatric care, this mainly comes up when pregnancy or postpartum nausea intersects with anxiety/depression treatment—so decisions are individualized and safety-focused.
sections.pregnancy: Ondansetron may be considered for severe or persistent nausea and vomiting of pregnancy when preferred agents have failed. Safety data are mixed; absolute risk appears low, but some guideline language recommends individualized decision-making—especially before 10 weeks gestation. Dose-dependent QT prolongation is also a consideration, so higher-risk patients may need ECG/electrolyte monitoring.
sections.lactation: Ondansetron is present in human milk. Available data suggest infant exposure is low and reported adverse events in studied infants were not observed; breastfeeding is often considered acceptable when the relative infant dose is <10%, but this should be individualized (especially for premature infants or medically fragile infants).
sections.geriatrics: No routine oral dose adjustment is generally required, but older adults may have higher baseline QT risk (more cardiac disease, more QT-prolonging meds). If QT risk factors exist, consider ECG/electrolyte monitoring.
sections.hepatic: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: typically no adjustment; severe hepatic impairment: do not exceed 8 mg/day total.
sections.renal: No dose adjustment is usually necessary because renal clearance accounts for a small fraction of total clearance; dialysis is unlikely to remove significant amounts.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: ECG when clinically indicated: congenital long-QT, history of arrhythmia, heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, older adults with multiple QT-risk meds, or if giving IV dosing.
Electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) when risk is present: ongoing vomiting/diarrhea, diuretics, malnutrition, or medical illness that increases QT vulnerability.
Serotonin syndrome symptoms when combined with serotonergic meds: agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, diarrhea, fever, hyperreflexia—stop and seek urgent care if suspected.
Hypersensitivity reactions: hives, swelling, wheezing, hypotension—medical emergency.
Bowel function: constipation monitoring, especially if the patient is already prone to constipation or is taking constipating medications (opioids, anticholinergics, some psych meds).
Functional outcome: Are you able to eat, hydrate, and stay on your primary psychiatric treatment plan?

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Formulation choice is mostly about how sick your stomach is and how fast you need relief.
items: Oral tablets: commonly 4 mg, 8 mg (some products include 24 mg tablets for specific medical protocols)
Orally disintegrating tablets (ODT): 4 mg, 8 mg (useful when swallowing is hard during nausea; dissolves on the tongue)
Oral solution: helpful for people who can’t swallow tablets or need flexible dosing
Injection (IV/IM): used in medical settings when oral dosing isn’t possible or rapid control is needed
Oral soluble film (Zuplenz): discontinued in the United States

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Ondansetron blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors—both in the gut (peripheral signals) and in the brain’s vomiting center (central signals). Translation: it turns down the serotonin-driven nausea reflex so the stomach-brain “vomit alarm” stops firing.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In psychiatry, ondansetron is a supportive care medication. It doesn’t treat anxiety, panic, depression, or insomnia directly—but it can keep nausea from wrecking adherence and recovery. It’s especially useful early in SSRI/SNRI treatment, during med switches, and in people whose anxiety lives in their GI tract. The main clinical decision points are: (1) do you actually need it regularly, or can you use it PRN, and (2) are there QT or serotonin-syndrome risks because of your other meds and medical history?

faqs.a: No—ondansetron (Zofran) is an anti-nausea medication. In psychiatry, it’s used as supportive care when nausea is getting in the way of treatment (like SSRI start-up nausea or anxiety/panic nausea).
Many people feel nausea relief within about 30 minutes. Oral forms often peak later (around a couple hours), but the symptom relief can start earlier.

faqs.q: Can Zofran help with nausea from SSRIs or SNRIs?
faqs.a: Yes—this is one of the most common psychiatry-adjacent uses. It can be used short-term or PRN to get you through the early nausea window so you can actually stay on the medication long enough to benefit.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Headache and constipation are the big two. Some people also feel a little dizzy or tired, especially if they’re dehydrated from nausea.

faqs.q: What’s the QT prolongation warning and why should I care?
faqs.a: QT prolongation is a change on an ECG that can increase the risk of dangerous heart rhythms (rare, but serious). The risk is higher with certain IV dosing and in people with risk factors—like electrolyte abnormalities, heart disease, bradycardia, congenital long-QT, or multiple QT-prolonging medications (which can happen in psychiatry).

faqs.q: Can I take ondansetron with antidepressants?
faqs.a: Often yes, but it depends on your specific meds and risk factors. Two things matter: (1) QT stacking if your antidepressant/antipsychotic also prolongs QT, and (2) serotonin syndrome risk—reported with 5-HT3 antagonists especially when combined with serotonergic agents. If you’re on multiple meds, have your clinician run an interaction check.

It’s rare, but serotonin syndrome has been reported with 5-HT3 antagonists, especially when combined with serotonergic medications (like SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs, mirtazapine, lithium, tramadol, fentanyl, methylene blue). If you develop agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle stiffness, diarrhea, or fever—get urgent medical help.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off Zofran?
faqs.a: No. Ondansetron doesn’t require tapering. You can usually stop when nausea resolves—unless your clinician has you on a specific scheduled protocol for a medical reason.
Usually not. Most people don’t feel sedated the way they might with promethazine or hydroxyzine. If you feel drowsy, it may be from dehydration, illness, or other medications in the mix.

faqs.q: Is ondansetron safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: This is individualized. Guidelines discuss ondansetron as an option for severe or persistent nausea and vomiting of pregnancy when preferred agents fail, and some guidance suggests extra caution/individualized decision-making early in pregnancy (e.g., before 10 weeks). It is present in breast milk, but available data suggest infant exposure is low. Talk through risks, benefits, and alternatives with your clinician.

faqs.q: What’s a practical PRN plan for psych-med nausea?
faqs.a: A common approach is 4 to 8 mg by mouth as needed, spaced out (often every 8 to 12 hours if symptoms persist). The goal is the lowest effective dose for the shortest time—especially if you’re on other QT-risk meds or have cardiac risk factors.
